question: On a 3x3 Rubik's Cube, how many non-top-facing stickers must be seen to fully identify the PLL case when solving using the CFOP method?

4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the answer is probably 5. With the 8 visible side stickers on the last layer (the non-U faces of the 4 edges and 4 corners), the permutations aren't fully independent, so a handful of them usually encodes the full case. In practice you can often nail it down by checking three edge positions plus two corner orientations/positions; the remaining possibilities collapse quickly because of how PLLs are structured, and the sixth sticker is typically redundant once those five are known.

5.text:
In CFOP the U-face is solved by the OLL step so that every U sticker is the
same colour.  The whole content of the last layer permutation is therefore
carried by the side of the U-layer.

The U-layer is made of 4 U-edges and 4 U-corners

* a U-edge has one U-sticker and one side-sticker, 4 side stickers;
* a U-corner has one U-sticker and two side-stickers, 8 side stickers.

Hence the U-layer carries

4×1+4×2 = 12

stickers which are not on U.  Those 12 stickers are the side colours of the
8 U-layer pieces.  In particular a piece is identified by its side colour
or colours: a U-edge is identified by its single side sticker and a U-corner
is identified by the unordered pair of its two side stickers.  One side
sticker per piece is enough for the permutation information, i.e. 4
edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 distinct piece identifiers,
which in the U-layer are the 12 physical non-U stickers.  That is the
information that is actually inspected in PLL recognition.  The 8 piece
identifiers are normally met as the 6 stickers that are visible on the
F and R faces of the U-layer and the remaining two are obtained by a
quarter turn of the cube. ∎

1.text:
In CFOP the U face is finished before PLL is started.  After OLL is done the
nine U stickers are all the same colour as the U centre so that the U face
itself carries no information about the permutation of the U layer.  All the
information about which U piece is sitting in which U position is carried
by the lateral colours of the U layer.

In the usual looking angle you see the U layer from an oblique view.  The
U layer has

* 4 U edges – 1 lateral sticker each, 4 stickers in all,
* 4 U corners – 2 lateral stickers each, 8 stickers in all,

12 lateral stickers in total.  Up to a rotation about the vertical axis the
permutation of the U layer is completely determined by the six lateral
stickers that belong to the two faces that meet at the front right corner,
three on the front top row and three on the right top row,  i.e. by the
four edge lateral stickers and two independent corner lateral stickers.
In the ordinary textbook picture this is quoted as the seven visible
lateral stickers of the U layer, 0 U stickers.  In particular no information
at all is ever taken from the nine U face stickers and the case can be read
off the side colours alone.  This is why PLL is normally said to be read
off the six – seven in the usual viewpoint – non-U stickers of the last
layer.  Up to symmetry the familiar figure is the six distinct lateral
positions, in practice the seven to eight lateral stickers you can see at
once, and no U face sticker is ever needed.

2.text:
In CFOP the U–layer is already oriented so the 9 stickers of the U face are
all the same colour and they carry no information at all about the
permutation.

Put the cube U up.  What is left of the U–layer is

* 4 U–edges.  After OLL each U–edge is oriented, it has one U sticker and
one side sticker.  The side colour of the edge is the whole identity of
the edge on the U–layer, 4 stickers;

* 4 U–corners.  After OLL each corner is oriented, it has one U sticker
and two side stickers.  The unordered pair of side colours is the
identity of the corner on the U–layer.  That is 2 side stickers per
corner, 8 stickers in all.

Hence the U–layer is completely described by the

4 + 2×4 = 12

side stickers of the U–layer, i.e. the 12 non–U stickers that belong to the
top layer.  Once those 12 stickers are known the four U–edges and the four
U–corners are known in their absolute positions and the 21 PLL classes up
to rotation are distinguished.  

In a single static view you see two adjacent side faces of the U–layer,
6 distinct non–U stickers, the 3 top-row stickers of the front face and
the 3 top-row stickers of the right face, and the 12 can be read by
turning the cube round.  This is the 8 side stickers normally spoken of
as the four edge colours + one side colour per corner that is enough for
ordinary recognition; the information theoretic worst case which makes the
permutation absolutely unique is the full 12 side stickers of the U–layer.
This is normally quoted as the 6 stickers you see on the two faces you are
looking at, 12 for the whole U–layer.

3.text:
In CFOP the U face is already colour solved after OLL so the U face itself
carries no permutation information.  All of the permutation information
of the last layer is carried by the side colours of the eight U-layer
pieces.

* 4 U-edges : the U-colour is known, the piece is identified by the
single side sticker that it shows on F,R,B,L.  4 stickers.
* 4 U-corners : the U-colour is known, a corner is identified by the
pair of side colours that it shows.  A corner can be identified by
either of its two side stickers, viz. the F- or R-sticker of UFR etc.
So one distinct identifier per corner is enough and the four corners
are identified by four distinct side stickers.

Hence in terms of piece identifiers you have to be able to read four
edge identifiers and four corner identifiers, i.e. eight distinct
U-layer side identifiers.  On the physical cube those eight identifiers
are the twelve stickers that belong to the U-layer but are not on the U
face

* 4 U-edges × 1 side sticker = 4 stickers
* 4 U-corners × 2 side stickers = 8 stickers
= 12 non-U stickers on the U-layer

which is the usual statement that the U-layer is read by its 12 side
stickers.  Up to the usual parity/elimination redundancy the permutation
of the four edges can be recovered from three edge stickers and the
permutation of the four corners from three corner stickers, i.e. seven
independent side stickers are enough to distinguish the 288 U-orientated
PLL states and the 21 PLL cases up to rotation.  This is the eight-piece
identifier, 12-physical-sticker, count that is normally quoted as ‘the
eight stickers of the U-layer’ and in information-theoretic terms
≈7 independent non-U stickers.

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: Round 0 synthesis

* Core CFOP fact agreed by all: after OLL the U face is solved, the 9 U stickers are all the same colour and carry zero permutation information. All PLL information is in the side colours of the U-layer.

* U-layer inventory:
  * 4 U-edges: 1 U + 1 side sticker each → 4 non-U stickers.
  * 4 U-corners: 1 U + 2 side stickers each → 8 non-U stickers.
  * Total non-U stickers belonging to the U-layer = 12. These 12 are the physical information carriers.

* What is normally inspected:
  * In a fixed oblique view you see two adjacent side faces of the U-layer. That is 3 top-row stickers per face = 6 physical stickers.
  * Those 6 are: UF front, UFL front, UFR front on Front, and UFR right, UR right, UBR right on Right, etc. The UFR corner is seen with two side stickers in that view.
  * By rotating the cube the other 6 non-U stickers can be brought into view. So the whole U-layer can be read from the 12 side stickers.

* Identification counting disagreement:
  * Piece-identifier view: 4 edge identifiers + 4 corner identifiers = 8 distinct piece identifiers. Physically that is the 12 stickers, 4 edges ×1 + 4 corners ×2.
  * Information-redundancy view: permutation of 4 items is fixed by 3 items. Hence 3 edge side stickers determine the 4th edge, and 3 corner identifiers determine the 4th corner. Colleague 3 notes this gives ~7 independent non-U stickers to distinguish the 288 U-oriented PLL states / 21 PLL cases up to rotation. 
  * Colleague 1 describes the same as the six lateral stickers of the two faces meeting at the front-right corner, i.e. four edge lateral stickers + two independent corner lateral stickers, commonly quoted as seven visible lateral stickers in the textbook picture, zero U stickers.
  * Colleague 2 stresses worst-case uniqueness: 12 side stickers of the U-layer are needed for an absolutely unique permutation; 6 are visible in one static view, 12 for the whole layer.

* Outlier claim:
  * Colleague 4 argues for ≈5 stickers being enough in practice, three edge positions + two corner positions collapsing the rest. This is the minimal heuristic claim vs the formal counts above.

* Open issues for me:
  * Is the question asking for minimal independent stickers in one static view, minimal independent identifiers irrespective of view, or total physical non-U stickers of the U-layer?
  * Disambiguation between counting physical stickers vs independent piece identifiers, and whether the UFR corner’s two visible side stickers should be counted as one identifier or two physical stickers.
  * The precise conventional number quoted in CFOP teaching: 6 visible / 7 independent / 8 identifiers / 12 physical.

Current working understanding: Zero U stickers are needed. The U-layer is completely described by its 12 non-U side stickers, 8 piece identifiers. In a normal view 6 physical stickers are seen, which is informationally ~7 independent stickers, enough to distinguish the 21 PLL cases up to rotation. The 12-sticker total is the information-theoretic worst case for absolute uniqueness.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is converging on the same structural fact and diverges only on how to count “must be seen”.

* After OLL the U-face is monochrome and carries no permutation information. All PLL information is carried by the side colours of the U-layer pieces.
* U-layer inventory: 4 U-edges ×1 side sticker = 4 stickers; 4 U-corners ×2 side stickers = 8 stickers. 4+8 =12 non-U stickers physically belong to the U-layer. That is the complete description of the last-layer permutation.
* Piece identifiers: an U-edge is identified by its single side colour, 4 identifiers; a U-corner is identified by the unordered pair of its two side colours, 4 identifiers. So 8 distinct piece identifiers, realised by the 12 physical side stickers.
* Viewpoint: in a static oblique view you see two adjacent side faces of the U-layer. That is the 3 top-row stickers of Front and the 3 top-row stickers of Right, i.e. 6 distinct non-U stickers at once, 12 in total if the cube is turned. The four edge side stickers and one side sticker per corner are the usual 8-sticker recognition set.
* Redundancy: up to rotation about the vertical axis the 21 PLL classes up to rotation are distinguished by fewer than the full 12. The usual textbook quote is 6–7 independent lateral stickers – the six stickers you see at once, seven independent in information-theoretic terms – e.g. four edge side stickers plus three independent corner side stickers. Colleague 4’s 5-sticker claim is the extreme minimal-information bound; the commonly quoted practical number is six visible / seven independent, 12 physical.

So the U layer is described by 12 non-U stickers, 8 piece identifiers, 6 stickers visible in a single view and ≈7 independent stickers are enough to distinguish the 21 PLL cases up to rotation. The literal total remains 12 non-U stickers on the U-layer.

* Colleague 4’s 5-sticker claim is an outlier; it confuses typical recognisability in practice with worst-case uniqueness and underestimates the need to resolve edge vs corner parity.

All colleagues agree no U-face sticker is ever needed. * Colleague 4’s “5 stickers” is an outlier; the consensus in the round is 12 physical non-U stickers on the U-layer, 6 stickers visible at once in the usual view, and ≈7 independent stickers in information-theoretic terms for a complete identification. * 4 U-corners : 1 U sticker + 2 side stickers per corner → 8 non-U side stickers, the unordered pair of side colours is the identifier of the corner

4 × 1 + 4 × 2 = 12

That is the worst-case unique identification.
